Macros Manual examples/nats_retry.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { // Five deliveries of one payment, the first included; the fifth that still fails goes // to "payments.dead" instead, payload and headers as they arrived. b.include(reconcile) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") .include(store) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") .include(on_dead_letter) }, ) } examples/manual/nats_retry.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { let stored = JetStreamSubject::new("payments.stored", "PAYMENTS").durable("reconciler"); // Five deliveries of one payment, the first included; the fifth that still fails goes // to "payments.dead" instead, payload and headers as they arrived. b.include(subscriber("payments.settled", Reconcile).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") .include(subscriber(stored, Reconcile).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") .include(subscriber("payments.dead", OnDeadLetter).build()) }, ) }

retry_after(delay) on JetStream puts the delay in the negative acknowledgement; on Core the framework publishes a copy after the delay. A JetStream consumer takes the delay as part of -NAK. The server holds the message for that long and delivers it again on the same consumer. Nothing is published, so the message keeps its stream sequence, and its delivery count rises by one. On a durable consumer the delayed message survives a restart of the service, because the server holds it. A Core subject has no acknowledgement to carry a delay. The framework waits out the delay in the service's memory and publishes a copy of the message, payload and headers, back to the subject the subscription reads. The copy carries RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, raised by one on every copy. A process that exits before the delay is over loses the copy. A CoreWildcard reads many subjects, so its mount site names where the copy goes with out_retry. A cap declared at the mount site ends the retries of one message.

A payment the ledger has not caught up with is checked again after 30 seconds, on a Core subject and on a stream. Macros Manual examples/nats_retry.rs /// The ledger has not caught up yet, so the delivery asks to come back later. On a Core subject /// the framework publishes a copy of the payment to the subject once the delay is over. #[subscriber("payments.settled")] async fn reconcile(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.settled { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "not settled yet, checking again later"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } /// The same work through a stream: the delay rides the negative acknowledgement, and the server /// holds the message and delivers it again on this consumer. #[subscriber(JetStreamSubject::new("payments.stored", "PAYMENTS").durable("reconciler"))] async fn store(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { if payment.settled { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "not settled yet, checking again later"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } examples/manual/nats_retry.rs /// The ledger has not caught up yet, so the delivery asks to come back later. Mounted on a Core /// subject, the framework publishes a copy of the payment to the subject once the delay is over; /// mounted on a stream consumer, the delay rides the negative acknowledgement and the server /// holds the message. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<Payment> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if payment.settled { return ready(Ok(())); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "not settled yet, checking again later"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK))) } }

A subject in #[subscriber] reads that Core NATS subject; a descriptor carries every other setting of its delivery model. #[subscriber("orders.created")] reads the subject orders.created over Core NATS, with no queue group. It is the same subscription as CoreSubject::new("orders.created"). Core NATS hands a message to whoever is subscribed at that moment and stores nothing, so a message published before the service starts never reaches it. Every other setting belongs to a descriptor, one type per delivery model: Descriptor Reads Its settings CoreSubject one Core NATS subject queue_group CoreWildcard every Core NATS subject a pattern matches queue_group JetStreamSubject a stream, through a pull consumer durable, filter_subject, deliver_policy, max_ack_pending, ack_wait, pull_expires A setting of the other model is not a method of the descriptor, so naming one does not compile. A descriptor goes where the subject goes, as the attribute's first argument. The manual form passes the subject, or the descriptor, to subscriber(source, body). The subscription's name is the subject the descriptor names: a test reads its deliveries under that name. All subscriptions of a service share the one connection of its NatsBroker.

The subject orders.created, read over Core NATS. Macros Manual examples/nats_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads the Core NATS subject `orders.created`. #[subscriber("orders.created")] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(place) }) } examples/manual/nats_subscriptions_name.rs /// Reads the Core NATS subject `orders.created`. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order placed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders.created", Place).build()) }) }

A slice handler takes a batch: one JetStream pull fetch of the mount site's size, or a Core NATS batch the client assembles. A handler over &[T] is a batch handler, and batch(n) at the mount site is its largest batch. On a JetStreamSubject one batch is one pull request: the consumer asks the server for up to n messages. The fetch ends once it holds n, or once pull_expires runs out with fewer, 5 seconds by default. pull_expires takes a NonZeroDuration, because a fetch that expires at once would spin. Core NATS has no batch on the wire, so the client collects up to n deliveries and closes a short batch 10 ms after its first one. One outcome settles every message of the batch. A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles message i with outcome i. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>, where Ok(()) acknowledges the batch and Err(outcomes) settles message by message.

Three orders waiting in the stream arrive in one call. Macros Manual examples/nats_subscriptions_batches.rs /// Reconciles up to 50 orders per call; a fetch that finds fewer closes after 300 ms. #[subscriber( JetStreamSubject::new("orders.*", "ORDERS") .durable("reconciler") .pull_expires(NonZeroDuration::from_millis(nonzero!(300))) )] async fn reconcile(orders: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { let total: u64 = orders.iter().map(|order| order.cents).sum(); tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), total, "orders reconciled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reconciliation", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(reconcile.batch(nonzero!(50))) }) } examples/manual/nats_subscriptions_batches.rs /// Reconciles up to 50 orders per call; a fetch that finds fewer closes after 300 ms. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<[Order]> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let total: u64 = orders.iter().map(|order| order.cents).sum(); tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), total, "orders reconciled"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reconciliation", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { let orders = JetStreamSubject::new("orders.*", "ORDERS") .durable("reconciler") .pull_expires(NonZeroDuration::from_millis(nonzero!(300))); b.include(subscriber(orders, Reconcile).batch(nonzero!(50)).build()) }, ) }

CoreSubject reads one Core NATS subject; it stores nothing, and a delayed copy of a delivery is published back to the subject itself. CoreSubject::new takes the subject, and its one setting is the queue group. The server delivers a message to every subscription on the subject at that moment and keeps nothing for later. A subject is published to and subscribed to under one name, so a delayed retry needs nothing from the mount site. A retry_after(delay) settles the delivery, and after the delay the runtime publishes a copy back to the subject. The copy waits in the service's memory, so a process that exits before the timer fires loses it. A subject with * or > in it is a pattern, which is CoreWildcard; CoreSubject given one stops the service at startup. An empty subject stops it too. A stream that keeps messages for a consumer is JetStreamSubject.

A payment the bank has not cleared yet comes back to payments.captured after 30 seconds. Macros Manual examples/nats_subscriptions_core.rs /// Books a cleared payment; one the bank has not cleared yet comes back in 30 seconds, as a copy /// published to `payments.captured` again. #[subscriber(CoreSubject::new("payments.captured"))] async fn book(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { if !payment.cleared { tracing::info!(payment.id, "not cleared yet, checking again later"); return HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment booked"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(book) }) } examples/manual/nats_subscriptions_core.rs /// Books a cleared payment; one the bank has not cleared yet comes back in 30 seconds, as a copy /// published to `payments.captured` again. struct Book; impl Handle<Payment> for Book { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if !payment.cleared { tracing::info!(payment.id, "not cleared yet, checking again later"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK))); } tracing::info!(payment.id, "payment booked"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(CoreSubject::new("payments.captured"), Book).build()) }) }

CoreWildcard reads every Core NATS subject a pattern matches, * for one token and > for the rest, and the mount site names where a delayed copy goes. A subject is a list of tokens separated by dots. orders.* matches orders.created and orders.cancelled, but not orders.eu.created. orders.> matches all three, and > alone matches every subject. CoreWildcard::new takes the pattern, and its one setting is the queue group. The subscription's name is the pattern itself. A pattern names many subjects and none of them in particular, so the crate does not choose where a delayed retry copy goes. The mount site names that subject with out_retry(Publish).to(subject). A registration over a pattern that names none stops the service at startup, with an error naming the subscription. A subject the pattern matches brings the copy back to the same handler.

Every one-token order event is audited, and a delayed copy goes to orders.audit. Macros Manual examples/nats_subscriptions_wildcard.rs /// Audits every one-token order event: `orders.created`, `orders.cancelled`, and the rest. #[subscriber(CoreWildcard::new("orders.*"))] async fn audit(event: &OrderEvent) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(event.order_id, "order event audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { // A pattern is no destination, so the mount site names where a delayed copy goes. b.include(audit).out_retry(Publish).to("orders.audit") }, ) } examples/manual/nats_subscriptions_wildcard.rs /// Audits every one-token order event: `orders.created`, `orders.cancelled`, and the rest. struct Audit; impl Handle<OrderEvent> for Audit { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderEvent, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(event.order_id, "order event audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { // A pattern is no destination, so the mount site names where a delayed copy goes. b.include(subscriber(CoreWildcard::new("orders.*"), Audit).build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("orders.audit") }, ) }

DeliverPolicy says where a newly created consumer starts: all, new, last, last per subject, a sequence or a time. deliver_policy sets it on the descriptor. The type is the one async-nats defines, re-exported by the crate. All, the default, starts with the oldest message the stream holds. New starts with the first message published after the consumer was created. Last starts with the newest message of the stream, and LastPerSubject with the newest message of each subject the filter matches. ByStartSequence starts at a stream sequence, and ByStartTime at the first message stored at or after a time. The policy applies once, when the consumer is created. A durable consumer that already exists resumes from its own position. An ephemeral consumer is created on every startup, so it starts from its policy each time.

A live ticker starts with the next price, and the prices the stream held before it started stay behind. Macros Manual examples/nats_subscriptions_deliver.rs /// A live ticker: each new consumer starts with the next price, not with the stream's history. #[subscriber(JetStreamSubject::new("prices.*", "PRICES").deliver_policy(DeliverPolicy::New))] async fn tick(price: &Price) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(price.product, price.cents, "price changed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ticker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(tick) }) } examples/manual/nats_subscriptions_deliver.rs /// A live ticker: each new consumer starts with the next price, not with the stream's history. struct Tick; impl Handle<Price> for Tick { fn handle( &self, price: &Price, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(price.product, price.cents, "price changed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn prices() -> JetStreamSubject { JetStreamSubject::new("prices.*", "PRICES").deliver_policy(DeliverPolicy::New) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ticker", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(prices(), Tick).build()) }) }

durable names a JetStream consumer: the server keeps its position across restarts, and subscriptions sharing it take messages in turn. A named consumer lives on the server, apart from any subscription. It remembers which messages were acknowledged, so a restarted service resumes after the last one and reads what arrived while it was down. A consumer without a name is ephemeral and starts from its deliver policy on every startup. Every replica of a service that reads through one durable shares its messages: each message goes to one of them, as in a queue group. At startup the subscription creates the consumer, or updates it when it exists. So the settings the last subscription opened with are the consumer's settings, and replicas that share a durable name one filter and one policy.

Every replica bills through the consumer billing, and a restarted service resumes where the consumer stopped. Macros Manual examples/nats_subscriptions_durable.rs /// Every replica reads through the consumer `billing`: each invoice is billed once, and a /// restarted service resumes where the consumer stopped. #[subscriber(JetStreamSubject::new("invoices.*", "INVOICES").durable("billing"))] async fn bill(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(bill) }) } examples/manual/nats_subscriptions_durable.rs /// Every replica reads through the consumer `billing`: each invoice is billed once, and a /// restarted service resumes where the consumer stopped. struct Bill; impl Handle<Invoice> for Bill { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(invoice.id, "invoice billed"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { let invoices = JetStreamSubject::new("invoices.*", "INVOICES").durable("billing"); b.include(subscriber(invoices, Bill).build()) }, ) }

filter_subject narrows the subjects of the stream a consumer reads; it defaults to the subject the descriptor names. A stream often stores several kinds of message under one prefix, such as every order event under orders.>. The consumer's filter decides which of them it is handed; the server skips the rest for this consumer. Without filter_subject the filter is the subject given to JetStreamSubject::new. With it, the descriptor's subject stays the subscription's name, and the filter decides what arrives. A filter may be a pattern with * and >. A durable consumer has one filter, the one its last subscription opened with.

The stream ORDERS stores every order event, and the refunds consumer reads orders.refunded only. Macros Manual examples/nats_subscriptions_filter.rs /// Reads only the refunds of the `ORDERS` stream, which stores every order event. #[subscriber( JetStreamSubject::new("orders.>", "ORDERS") .durable("refunds") .filter_subject("orders.refunded") )] async fn refund(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order refunded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(refund) }) } examples/manual/nats_subscriptions_filter.rs /// Reads only the refunds of the `ORDERS` stream, which stores every order event. struct Refund; impl Handle<Order> for Refund { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order refunded"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("refunds", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { let refunds = JetStreamSubject::new("orders.>", "ORDERS") .durable("refunds") .filter_subject("orders.refunded"); b.include(subscriber(refunds, Refund).build()) }, ) }

JetStreamSubject reads a stream through a pull consumer; the stream exists on the server before the service starts. A stream stores the messages published to its subjects, and a consumer reads them at its own pace. JetStreamSubject::new(subject, stream) takes the subject to read and the name of the stream that stores it. At startup the subscription finds the stream and creates its consumer; a stream the server does not have stops the service. The crate creates no stream: the service's deployment does, for example with nats stream add. Without durable the consumer is ephemeral, and the server discards it once the subscription closes. Each delivery settles on the server: an ack acknowledges it, and a retry or a delay is a negative acknowledgement the server acts on. The settings and their defaults: Setting Default What it does durable none, an ephemeral consumer names the consumer, which keeps its position across restarts filter_subject the subject narrows what the consumer reads from the stream deliver_policy DeliverPolicy::All where a new consumer starts max_ack_pending 1024 how many deliveries the consumer holds unacknowledged ack_wait 30 seconds how long the server waits for a settlement before it delivers again pull_expires 5 seconds how long one fetch of a batch waits for messages The subscription's name is the subject the descriptor names. A delivery carries its place in the stream, which a handler reads through the context keys.

The stream ORDERS stores orders.*, and an ephemeral consumer reads it. Macros Manual examples/nats_subscriptions_jetstream.rs /// Reads `orders.*` from the stream `ORDERS`; the ack settles each order on the server. #[subscriber(JetStreamSubject::new("orders.*", "ORDERS"))] async fn ship(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(ship) }) } examples/manual/nats_subscriptions_jetstream.rs /// Reads `orders.*` from the stream `ORDERS`; `Ok` acknowledges each order on the server. struct Ship; impl Handle<Order> for Ship { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order shipped"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shipping", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { let orders = JetStreamSubject::new("orders.*", "ORDERS"); b.include(subscriber(orders, Ship).build()) }, ) }

The nats-partition-key header keys the lanes of workers(n, by_key): messages sharing a key run on one lane, in order. workers(n, by_key) runs n sequential lanes in one subscription. Messages with one key run in order on one lane, and different keys run at once. NATS has no partitions or message keys, so the key travels in the nats-partition-key header. The sender sets it: any NATS client writes the header, and a RustStream message type declares it in its typed header contract. The value is text, because a NATS header is; a value that is not a single line of UTF-8 fails the publish. A message without the header has no key and rotates over the lanes. The lanes work the same on Core NATS and on a stream. The manual form writes the lanes as workers_by_key(n) on the mount chain.

Two tenants' orders, each order a second of work: the tenants run side by side, two seconds in all. Macros Manual examples/nats_subscriptions_keys.rs /// Eight lanes keyed by the partition-key header: one tenant's orders run in order, different /// tenants at once. #[subscriber(CoreSubject::new("orders.placed"), workers(8, by_key))] async fn place(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { process(order).await; HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(place) }) } examples/manual/nats_subscriptions_keys.rs /// Eight lanes keyed by the partition-key header: one tenant's orders run in order, different /// tenants at once. struct Place; impl Handle<Order> for Place { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { process(order).await; Ok(()) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { let placed = CoreSubject::new("orders.placed"); b.include( subscriber(placed, Place) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(8)) .build(), ) }, ) }

max_ack_pending caps how many unacknowledged deliveries the server lets a consumer hold at once; the default is 1024. A delivery is pending from the moment the server hands it out until it is settled. Once the consumer holds that many, the server stops delivering until a settlement frees a place. The cap belongs to the consumer, so every subscription that shares a durable counts against one cap. It bounds the work in flight from the server's side, whatever the service does. workers(n) runs up to n handlers at once in one subscription; with a cap below n, the cap is the limit. A delivery the consumer holds counts against its ack_wait from the moment it is handed out, so a large cap over slow handlers lets deliveries wait out their ack_wait and come back. The cap is enforced by the server, so a test of it runs against a live server.

Six workers render reports, and the server hands out two at a time. Macros Manual examples/nats_subscriptions_pending.rs /// Six workers, but the server hands out at most two reports before they are acknowledged, so /// two render at a time. #[subscriber( JetStreamSubject::new("reports.requested", "REPORTS") .durable("renderers") .max_ack_pending(2), workers(6) )] async fn produce(report: &Report) -> HandlerOutcome { render(report).await; HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reports", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(produce) }) } examples/manual/nats_subscriptions_pending.rs /// Six workers, but the server hands out at most two reports before they are acknowledged, so /// two render at a time. struct Produce; impl Handle<Report> for Produce { async fn handle( &self, report: &Report, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { render(report).await; Ok(()) } } fn reports() -> JetStreamSubject { JetStreamSubject::new("reports.requested", "REPORTS") .durable("renderers") .max_ack_pending(2) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reports", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(subscriber(reports(), Produce).workers(nonzero!(6)).build()) }) }

queue_group puts a Core NATS subscription in a queue group: each message goes to one member, and one name is one group across subjects. Without a group, every subscription on a subject receives every message. Replicas of a service that subscribe in one group share the messages instead, and the server picks one member for each. A subscription outside the group still receives everything, so an audit can read beside the workers. The server keys a group by its name alone, so subscriptions with one group name on two subjects or patterns are one group. A message both of them match is delivered once, to one member. CoreSubject::queue_group and CoreWildcard::queue_group take the same name. Core NATS keeps nothing for a group: a message published while no member is subscribed is lost. On a stream the same sharing comes from a durable consumer that several subscriptions read through.

Every replica fulfils orders in the group fulfilment, and the audit reads every order outside it. Macros Manual examples/nats_subscriptions_queue.rs /// Every replica of the service joins `fulfilment`, so each order is fulfilled once. #[subscriber(CoreSubject::new("orders.created").queue_group("fulfilment"))] async fn fulfil(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order fulfilled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Outside the group: the audit reads every order. #[subscriber(CoreWildcard::new("orders.*"))] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("fulfilment", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(fulfil) .include(audit) .out_retry(Publish) .to("orders.audit") }, ) } examples/manual/nats_subscriptions_queue.rs /// Every replica of the service joins `fulfilment`, so each order is fulfilled once. struct Fulfil; impl Handle<Order> for Fulfil { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order fulfilled"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Outside the group: the audit reads every order. struct Audit; impl Handle<Order> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("fulfilment", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { let fulfilment = CoreSubject::new("orders.created").queue_group("fulfilment"); b.include(subscriber(fulfilment, Fulfil).build()) .include(subscriber(CoreWildcard::new("orders.*"), Audit).build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("orders.audit") }, ) }

TestApp::start connects NatsBroker in process: subjects, queue groups, streams, consumers and request-reply, with no server. A test hands the harness the app main runs, unchanged, and addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<NatsBroker>(). The testing feature in [dev-dependencies] adds the in-process mode, and turns on the core's harness with it. The in-process mode has no settings of its own. It parses the addresses as the client parses them, so an address the client refuses fails TestApp::start. It reads the two connection options that change what the server delivers, no_echo and the inbox prefix. It routes as a server routes. A Core NATS subscription receives every subject its subject or pattern matches, and a queue group hands each message to one of its members. A stream stores what its consumers' filter subjects place in it, and a stream a subscription names is there for it. A consumer starts where its deliver policy says, numbers its deliveries, and fills every key of the JetStream context. A JetStream delivery is acknowledged, redelivered, terminated or held for a delay as on a server, and one left unsettled comes back after its ack_wait. A Core NATS delivery has no acknowledgement and is never redelivered. A request to a subject nobody reads fails at once with "no responders". It refuses what a server refuses: a subject with whitespace, a header with no NATS form, a message over the 1 MiB payload limit, a JetStream publish no stream stores, an expectation that does not hold, and every publish after the broker shut down. What only a server has is for a live test: a stream's own subject list and limits, a stream the server lacks, max_ack_pending, authentication and TLS, and the connect itself. A publish through the harness returns once every handler it woke has settled, a reply included. The assertions that follow read finished state.

The dependency line: [dev-dependencies] ruststream-nats = { version = "0.8", features = ["testing"] } The tests publish a payment and read how the handler settled it. TestApp::start_live runs the same test body against a running NATS server, for what only a server has. It connects the broker through its ordinary connect, so startup dials the server and every JetStream subscription looks up its stream there. The body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most, and start_live_within sets another bound. The live mode is for what the in-process mode leaves to the server: a stream's own subject list and limits, a stream the server lacks failing startup, max_ack_pending, authentication and TLS, and the timing of the connect. A stream is the server's state, and the server keeps what earlier runs left in it. So a test creates the stream through an admin connection's jetstream before the app starts, replacing a leftover, and deletes it afterwards. In the example, live::url returns the server's address from NATS_TEST_URL, and the test returns early without one, so cargo test passes on a machine with no server. A job that stood a server up sets RUSTSTREAM_REQUIRE_LIVE=1, and a missing address then fails the test instead of skipping it. The repository's stand is docker-compose.test.yml, a NATS server with JetStream that just brokers-up starts.

The two tests share one body: one in process, one against the server at NATS_TEST_URL. This guide settles JetStream deliveries with the handler's outcome, sizes ack_wait for slow handlers, handles a message delivered twice, and shows what Core NATS does not promise. A handler settles its delivery with the value it returns, and the runtime sends the settlement after the handler. On a JetStream consumer each outcome is an acknowledgement the server acts on: Outcome Sent to the server What the server does ack +ACK forgets the message for this consumer retry -NAK delivers it again at once retry_after(delay) -NAK with the delay holds it and delivers it again after the delay drop +TERM never delivers it again no settlement nothing delivers it again after ack_wait A redelivery keeps the message's stream sequence, and the server counts its deliveries. The example is a payments service. It captures authorized payments through the bank and announces each capture to a dashboard.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long a busy bank asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments.authorized")] struct Payment { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments.captured")] struct Captured { payment: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber( JetStreamSubject::new("payments.authorized", "PAYMENTS") .durable("capture") .ack_wait(NonZeroDuration::from_secs(nonzero!(60))), reply )] async fn capture( payment: &Payment, Ctx(delivered): Ctx<Delivered>, State(bank): State<Arc<Bank>>, ) -> Result<Captured, HandlerOutcome> { if delivered.is_some_and(|count| count > 1) { tracing::info!(payment.id, ?delivered, "payment delivered again"); } match bank.capture(payment).await { Ok(()) => Ok(Captured { payment: payment.id, amount_cents: payment.amount_cents, }), // Past the rate limit: the server holds the payment and delivers it after the delay. Err(Refusal::Busy) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)), // No answer: the server delivers the payment again at once. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), // The server never delivers a terminated payment again. Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "card declined, payment terminated"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } src/main.rs /// How long a busy bank asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Payment { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Payment { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payments.authorized"; } impl MessageHeaders for Payment { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Payment { const NAME: &'static str = "Payment"; } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Captured { payment: u64, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Captured { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payments.captured"; } impl MessageHeaders for Captured { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Captured { const NAME: &'static str = "Captured"; } struct Capture; impl Handle<Payment, Captured, (), JetStreamContext, Clients> for Capture { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, JetStreamContext, Clients>, ) -> Result<Captured, HandlerOutcome> { let delivered = ctx.context(DELIVERED); if delivered.is_some_and(|count| count > 1) { tracing::info!(payment.id, ?delivered, "payment delivered again"); } match ctx.state().bank.capture(payment).await { Ok(()) => Ok(Captured { payment: payment.id, amount_cents: payment.amount_cents, }), // Past the rate limit: the server holds the payment and delivers it after the delay. Err(Refusal::Busy) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF)), // No answer: the server delivers the payment again at once. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), // The server never delivers a terminated payment again. Err(Refusal::Declined) => { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "card declined, payment terminated"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } } The bank answers in four ways, and each needs a different outcome. A capture returns Captured, which the runtime publishes as the reply and then acknowledges the payment. Busy means the bank's rate limit is used up, so the payment waits 30 seconds on the server. Unavailable means the bank did not answer, so the payment comes back at once. Declined means the card cannot be charged, and another try gets the same answer, so the payment is terminated. A retry without a cap comes back forever; Retries and dead letters adds the cap and a dead-letter subject.

JetStream delivers at least once. A payment comes back after a retry, after ack_wait ran out, and after a process stopped before it settled. So a handler sees some payments twice, and its work has to accept a repeat. Here the bank takes the payment id as an idempotency key and charges a repeated capture once. Ctx<Delivered> is the server's delivery count, 1 on the first delivery, and capture logs a payment it sees again.

The server waits ack_wait for a settlement, 30 seconds unless the descriptor names another. After that it delivers the message again, while the first handler may still run. capture sets 60 seconds, above the longest time the bank takes to answer. Set ack_wait above the worst time of the handler, and the two deliveries never overlap. An expired ack_wait also counts as a delivery for the attempt cap.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber("payments.captured")] async fn refresh(captured: &Captured) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(captured.payment, "dashboard refreshed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Refresh; impl Handle<Captured, (), (), (), Clients> for Refresh { fn handle( &self, captured: &Captured, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(captured.payment, "dashboard refreshed"); ready(Ok(())) } } refresh reads the captures on a Core NATS subject. Core NATS delivers at most once and has no acknowledgement. Settling a Core delivery reports AckError::Unsupported, and the runtime logs it as a warning. A Core message the process loses is gone, and nothing brings it back. The dashboard can lose an update, because the next capture refreshes it again. A payment cannot, so payments travel through a stream.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(capture).include(refresh) }) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = Clients> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| Ok::<_, Infallible>(Clients::default())) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include( subscriber( JetStreamSubject::new("payments.authorized", "PAYMENTS") .durable("capture") .ack_wait(NonZeroDuration::from_secs(nonzero!(60))), Capture, ) .reply() .build(), ) .include(subscriber("payments.captured", Refresh).build()) }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The bank's client is the app's state, opened once at startup. A batch handler settles its whole batch with one outcome, or each message on its own when it returns Vec<HandlerOutcome>. The tests in the example file run the app in process with a paused clock, so the 30 seconds of Busy pass at once.
This guide installs ruststream-nats, starts a local NATS server and runs a first service against it.

Cargo.toml [dependencies] ruststream = { version = "0.8", features = ["macros", "json", "logging"] } ruststream-nats = "0.8" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } tracing = "0.1" [dev-dependencies] ruststream-nats = { version = "0.8", features = ["testing"] } tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt"] } ruststream is the framework: macros gives the attributes, json the default codec, and logging prints the service's log to the terminal. ruststream-nats is the NATS broker. Its testing feature adds the in-process NATS that tests run on. The broker crate has two features, both off by default: Feature What it gives testing the in-process NATS behind TestApp asyncapi the NATS bindings in the generated AsyncAPI document The client underneath is async-nats, written in Rust with TLS through rustls, so the build needs no system libraries.

One NATS server with JetStream is enough to develop against: compose.yaml services: nats: image: nats:2-alpine command: ["-js"] ports: - "4222:4222" docker compose up -d The server listens on localhost:4222. -js turns on JetStream, the streams that the guides from Streams and consumers on read and write. The examples publish with the NATS command-line tool, nats.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber("orders.created")] async fn take_order(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(take_order) }) } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Order { id: u64, amount_cents: u64, } struct TakeOrder; impl Handle<Order> for TakeOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.amount_cents == 0 { tracing::warn!(order.id, "order without an amount dropped"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(order.id, order.amount_cents, "order taken"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders.created", TakeOrder).build()) }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } take_order reads JSON orders from the Core NATS subject orders.created. It takes an order with an amount and drops one without. NatsBroker::new takes the server address and only records it. The connection opens when the service starts. #[ruststream::app] turns app into main; in the manual form, run_main does the same. Run the service: cargo run -- run Publish an order from another terminal: nats pub orders.created '{"id":1,"amount_cents":1250}' The service logs order taken with the order's id. Core NATS has no acknowledgement, so the log also shows ack / nack failed for each order: the runtime reports that the delivery could not be settled. Acknowledgement and delivery guarantees explains when that matters and how a stream settles each message. Ctrl+C stops the service. cargo generate scaffolds the same kind of service with a router: cargo generate --git https://github.com/powersemmi/ruststream-nats templates/nats --name my-service templates/nats-js scaffolds a service that reads a stream through a durable consumer.

The example file also holds two tests. Each starts the same app with TestApp::start, publishes an order and checks how take_order settled it. NatsBroker connects to an in-process NATS there, so the tests need no server: cargo test Testing a NATS service walks through such tests and what the in-process NATS models.

A service on async-nats writes its own subscription loops and publishes by hand. Here is where each part goes in RustStream: async-nats RustStream async_nats::connect or ConnectOptions::connect NatsBroker::new, with with_options for the ConnectOptions client.subscribe and a while let Some(message) loop a #[subscriber("subject")] handler client.queue_subscribe CoreSubject::queue_group (Subjects, wildcards and queue groups) serde_json::from_slice(&message.payload) the handler's parameter type, decoded by the codec client.publish a reply or an Out parameter, sent through the Publish policy client.request request on an Out<impl RequestReply, _> slot (Request-reply) create_consumer on a stream and a messages() loop JetStreamSubject (Streams and consumers) message.ack(), AckKind::Nak, AckKind::Term the handler's outcome: ack, retry, retry_after, drop (Acknowledgement and delivery guarantees) jetstream.publish and its acknowledgement JetStreamPublish (Publishing to streams)

A production cluster has several servers, asks the service who it is, and speaks TLS. Every one of these is a setting of the async-nats ConnectOptions, which the broker takes before anything is dialled.

src/main.rs /// Where the cluster is and who the service is, as the deployment provides them. struct Deployment { /// One server address or a comma-separated list. servers: String, /// The contents of the service's `.creds` file: its user JWT and its `NKey` seed. creds: String, /// The certificate authority that signed the servers' certificates. ca: PathBuf, } impl Deployment { fn from_env() -> io::Result<Self> { let var = |name: &str| { env::var(name).map_err(|_| io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::NotFound, name.to_owned())) }; Ok(Self { servers: var("NATS_SERVERS")?, creds: fs::read_to_string(var("NATS_CREDS")?)?, ca: var("NATS_CA")?.into(), }) } } fn broker(deployment: Deployment) -> io::Result<NatsBroker> { let options = ConnectOptions::with_credentials(&deployment.creds)? .add_root_certificates(deployment.ca) .require_tls(true) .name("orders") .connection_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10)); Ok(NatsBroker::new(deployment.servers).with_options(options)) } Cargo.toml [dependencies] async-nats = "0.50" The deployment provides the servers and two file paths in environment variables. NatsBroker::new takes one address or a comma-separated list, and the client picks one of them to connect to. with_options attaches the ConnectOptions and still dials nothing. A .creds file holds a user JWT and its NKey seed, which is how Synadia Cloud and the accounts set up with nsc identify a service. The app reads the file and hands its contents to ConnectOptions::with_credentials, which parses them at once. ConnectOptions::with_credentials_file reads the file itself, but it is async, and the app is built in a synchronous function. A file that does not parse stops the service before it connects. A server set up with a user and a password takes ConnectOptions::with_user_and_password, with a token with_token, and with an NKey alone with_nkey. add_root_certificates names the certificate authority that signed the servers' certificates, and require_tls refuses a connection without TLS. add_client_certificate adds the service's own certificate where the cluster asks for mutual TLS. The client reads certificate files when it connects. name shows the service in the server's monitoring, and connection_timeout bounds each attempt to connect.

The runtime connects at startup. After that the client reconnects on its own when a server goes away and restores the subscriptions. The generated AsyncAPI document reports each server's host and port, never the credentials. A client built outside the framework, such as one shared with other code of the process, becomes the connected broker with ConnectedNatsBroker::from_client. Only the plain NatsBroker fits the synchronous app function, so with_options is the way wherever it can express the setting.

The tests start the production service with the production broker, given test credentials, under TestApp::start. The in-process NATS parses the addresses as the client does and dials nothing, so the credentials and the certificate path never reach a server. A second test hands broker a .creds file that does not parse and expects the error. Authentication and TLS themselves happen only on a real cluster.

This guide publishes replies and messages into JetStream streams, stores a repeated message once, and refuses a write made from a stale version. A plain publish goes out over Core NATS and nobody confirms it. JetStreamPublish waits for the stream to acknowledge each message. So a message the stream refuses is an error the handler sees, not a silent loss. The example is an orders service. It confirms each order, archives it, and keeps the history of each customer account. The streams it writes to exist on the server: nats stream add ORDERS --subjects 'orders.placed' --defaults nats stream add CONFIRMATIONS --subjects 'confirmations.orders' --defaults nats stream add ARCHIVE --subjects 'archive.orders' --defaults nats stream add ACCOUNTS --subjects 'accounts.*' --defaults

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "confirmations.orders")] struct Confirmation { order: u64, } #[subscriber( JetStreamSubject::new("orders.placed", "ORDERS").durable("confirmer"), reply )] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); Confirmation { order: order.id } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Confirmation { order: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Confirmation { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "confirmations.orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for Confirmation { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Confirmation { const NAME: &'static str = "Confirmation"; } struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order confirmed"); ready(Ok(Confirmation { order: order.id })) } } confirm answers each order with a Confirmation on confirmations.orders. The app below sends that reply through JetStreamPublish::default().expect_stream("CONFIRMATIONS"). expect_stream names the stream that must store the subject, and a publish that another stream would take is refused. The order is acknowledged only after the stream has stored its confirmation. A refused confirmation fails the delivery, and the order comes back. The reply's subject is outside the ORDERS subjects. A reply stored in the stream a handler reads would reach that handler again.

This guide asks another service over NATS and waits for its answer, answers requests on their inbox, handles a request nobody answers, and scales the answering side. NATS correlates a reply with its request itself. A request carries an inbox, a subject unique to it, and the answer is published to that inbox. The example is two services in one app. The pricing service answers questions about prices, and the orders service asks it for the price of each order.

This guide retries a delivery now or later, caps the attempts and keeps what keeps failing in a dead-letter stream, on a stream consumer, a Core subject and a pattern. NATS has no dead-letter mechanism. JetStream can cap the deliveries of a message, but it sends the last one nowhere. So the mount site declares the cap and the dead-letter subject, and the framework applies them to both models. The example is a payments service that settles payments and sends refunds through a bank. It keeps its dead letters in a stream of their own: nats stream add PAYMENTS --subjects 'payments.settle' --defaults nats stream add DEAD --subjects 'dead.*' --defaults

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// How long a busy bank asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); /// The outcome a refusal of the bank calls for. fn outcome(refusal: Refusal) -> HandlerOutcome { match refusal { // Past the rate limit: a call right now would be refused again. Refusal::Busy => HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Refusal::Unavailable => HandlerOutcome::retry(), Refusal::Declined => HandlerOutcome::drop(), } } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments.settle")] struct Payment { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(JetStreamSubject::new("payments.settle", "PAYMENTS").durable("settler"))] async fn settle(payment: &Payment, State(bank): State<Arc<Bank>>) -> HandlerOutcome { match bank.charge(&payment.card).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(refusal) => { tracing::warn!(payment.id, ?refusal, "payment refused by the bank"); outcome(refusal) } } } src/main.rs /// How long a busy bank asks its callers to wait. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); /// The outcome a refusal of the bank calls for. fn outcome(refusal: Refusal) -> HandlerOutcome { match refusal { // Past the rate limit: a call right now would be refused again. Refusal::Busy => HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF), // No answer: try again at once, up to the attempt cap. Refusal::Unavailable => HandlerOutcome::retry(), Refusal::Declined => HandlerOutcome::drop(), } } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Payment { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Payment { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payments.settle"; } impl MessageHeaders for Payment { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Payment { const NAME: &'static str = "Payment"; } struct Settle; impl Handle<Payment, (), (), (), Clients> for Settle { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match ctx.state().bank.charge(&payment.card).await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), Err(refusal) => { tracing::warn!(payment.id, ?refusal, "payment refused by the bank"); Err(outcome(refusal)) } } } } outcome turns the bank's refusal into the handler's outcome. A busy bank is asked again in 30 seconds with retry_after. On a JetStream consumer the delay travels in the negative acknowledgement: the server holds the payment and delivers it again on the same consumer, with the same stream sequence. Nothing is published, and a process that stops in between loses nothing. A silent bank is asked again at once with retry, and a declined card is dropped.

On a JetStream consumer the count is the server's own, so an ack_wait that ran out counts too. The fifth delivery is not retried: dead_letter publishes it to dead.payments, payload and headers as they arrived. A dropped payment settles and goes nowhere, so the dead letters hold only the payments that ran out of attempts. A capped consumer without a dead-letter subject terminates its last delivery. dead.payments is a plain publish, and Core NATS keeps nothing nobody reads. The DEAD stream stores it, so a dead letter waits until someone looks at it. No subject the app reads matches a dead-letter subject, or a spent delivery would come back to the handler that gave up on it.

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(JetStreamSubject::new("dead.payments", "DEAD").durable("review"))] async fn review(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::error!(payment.id, "payment needs a person to look at it"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Review; impl Handle<Payment, (), (), (), Clients> for Review { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::error!(payment.id, "payment needs a person to look at it"); ready(Ok(())) } } review reads the dead payments from the DEAD stream like any other stream and logs each for a person to look at.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } #[subscriber(CoreWildcard::new("refunds.*"))] async fn send_refund(refund: &Refund, State(bank): State<Arc<Bank>>) -> HandlerOutcome { match bank.charge(&refund.card).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(refusal) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, ?refusal, "refund refused by the bank"); outcome(refusal) } } } src/main.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Refund { id: u64, card: String, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Refund { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Refund { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Refund { const NAME: &'static str = "Refund"; } struct SendRefund; impl Handle<Refund, (), (), (), Clients> for SendRefund { async fn handle( &self, refund: &Refund, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), Clients>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { match ctx.state().bank.charge(&refund.card).await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), Err(refusal) => { tracing::warn!(refund.id, ?refusal, "refund refused by the bank"); Err(outcome(refusal)) } } } } Core NATS cannot hold a message back. On a Core subscription a retry is a copy of the delivery that the framework publishes: retry publishes it at once, retry_after when the delay ends. The copy carries the delivery count in its x-ruststream-retry-count header, which the cap reads. A delayed copy is at most once: a process that stops before the delay ends loses it. A CoreSubject publishes its copies to its own subject. send_refund reads the pattern refunds.*, which has no single subject to publish to. So the app names one with out_retry(Publish).to("refunds.retry"), a subject the pattern matches, and the copies come back to send_refund. A registration over a pattern without it refuses to start, whether its handler retries or not. The third delivery of a refund goes to dead.refunds, with its count in the header. The tests in the example file run the app in process with a paused clock, so tb.advance(BACKOFF) lets the 30 seconds pass at once. Testing a NATS service covers the harness.

This guide reads a JetStream stream through durable and ephemeral consumers, chooses where a new consumer starts, reads the metadata of a delivery and takes messages in batches. A stream stores the messages published to its subjects, each under a sequence number. A consumer reads a stream at its own pace and acknowledges message by message. The example is a shop. It fulfils new orders, shows every order event on a dashboard, and reconciles paid orders with the bank.

A stream is the server's state. The service finds it at startup and never creates it, so create it once with the NATS command-line tool: nats stream add ORDERS --subjects 'orders.*' --defaults ORDERS stores every message published to orders.created, orders.paid and any other subject that orders.* matches. A plain publish to such a subject is stored, whoever publishes it. A subscription to a stream the server does not have fails the service's start.

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// What the warehouse is asked to ship. The sequence is the order's place in the stream. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "shipments.requested")] struct Shipment { order: u64, sequence: Option<u64>, } #[subscriber( JetStreamSubject::new("orders.created", "ORDERS").durable("fulfilment"), reply )] async fn fulfil(order: &Order, Ctx(sequence): Ctx<StreamSequence>) -> Shipment { tracing::info!(order.id, ?sequence, "order sent to the warehouse"); Shipment { order: order.id, sequence, } } src/main.rs /// What the warehouse is asked to ship. The sequence is the order's place in the stream. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Shipment { order: u64, sequence: Option<u64>, } impl OutgoingDestination for Shipment { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "shipments.requested"; } impl MessageHeaders for Shipment { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl MessageInfo for Shipment { const NAME: &'static str = "Shipment"; } struct Fulfil; impl Handle<Order, Shipment, (), JetStreamContext> for Fulfil { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, JetStreamContext>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Shipment, HandlerOutcome>> { let sequence = ctx.context(STREAM_SEQUENCE); tracing::info!(order.id, ?sequence, "order sent to the warehouse"); ready(Ok(Shipment { order: order.id, sequence, })) } } JetStreamSubject takes the subject the consumer reads and the stream that stores it. The subject is the consumer's filter, so fulfil reads only orders.created out of ORDERS. filter_subject sets another filter where the two should differ. The service creates the consumer when it starts, with every setting of the descriptor. durable names the consumer fulfilment. The server keeps its position, so a restarted service continues where it stopped. Replicas of the service share the one durable consumer, and each message goes to one of them. That is the JetStream counterpart of a queue group. The handler reads the delivery's place in the stream with Ctx<StreamSequence>. The JetStream context also carries the stream and consumer names, the consumer sequence, the delivery count and the number of messages still pending. In the manual form the handler takes Context<'_, JetStreamContext> and reads the same keys with ctx.context(..). On a Core NATS delivery every key reads None.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(JetStreamSubject::new("orders.*", "ORDERS").deliver_policy(DeliverPolicy::New))] async fn show(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order event on the dashboard"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Show; impl Handle<Order> for Show { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order event on the dashboard"); ready(Ok(())) } } A descriptor without durable creates an ephemeral consumer. Each process gets its own, and the server removes it after the subscription closes. So every replica of the service shows every order event. DeliverPolicy says where a new consumer starts. All, the default, starts at the first message the stream holds, and New at the next message published. Last, LastPerSubject, ByStartSequence and ByStartTime start at the last message, the last message of each subject, a sequence number or a point in time. The policy applies once, when the consumer is created; after that a durable consumer resumes from its own position.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber( JetStreamSubject::new("orders.paid", "ORDERS") .durable("reconciler") .pull_expires(NonZeroDuration::from_secs(nonzero!(1))) )] async fn reconcile(orders: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { let total: u64 = orders.iter().map(|order| order.amount_cents).sum(); tracing::info!(orders = orders.len(), total, "paid orders reconciled"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Reconcile; impl Handle<[Order]> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { let total: u64 = orders.iter().map(|order| order.amount_cents).sum(); tracing::info!(orders = orders.len(), total, "paid orders reconciled"); ready(Ok(())) } } A handler that takes &[Order] gets a batch of messages and runs once for the whole batch. The returned outcome settles every message of it.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(fulfil) .include(show) .include(reconcile.batch(nonzero!(100))) }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include( subscriber( JetStreamSubject::new("orders.created", "ORDERS").durable("fulfilment"), Fulfil, ) .reply() .build(), ) .include( subscriber( JetStreamSubject::new("orders.*", "ORDERS").deliver_policy(DeliverPolicy::New), Show, ) .build(), ) .include( subscriber( JetStreamSubject::new("orders.paid", "ORDERS") .durable("reconciler") .pull_expires(NonZeroDuration::from_secs(nonzero!(1))), Reconcile, ) .batch(nonzero!(100usize)) .build(), ) }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } The mount site names the batch size: batch(100) asks the server for up to a hundred messages in one pull. pull_expires on the descriptor says how long a pull waits for them, here one second, after which a smaller batch is handed over. The default is five seconds. The reply of fulfil is published over Core NATS, the broker's default. Publishing to streams stores replies in a stream instead. Core and JetStream subscriptions share one connection, so one service mixes both models freely. max_ack_pending caps how many deliveries a consumer holds unacknowledged; the default is 1024. Acknowledgement and delivery guarantees covers how each delivery settles.

This guide names Core NATS subjects, reads many of them with a wildcard, shares the work between replicas in a queue group and keeps the order of each key in parallel lanes. A subject is a name of tokens separated by dots, such as orders.eu.created. Core NATS hands a message to every subscription whose subject matches at that moment, and stores nothing. The example is an orders service. It packs the European orders, bills them, and audits every order event of every region.

pack reads orders.eu.created. The service runs in several replicas, and each order must be packed once. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(CoreSubject::new("orders.eu.created").queue_group("packers"))] async fn pack(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order packed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Pack; impl Handle<Order> for Pack { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order packed"); ready(Ok(())) } } CoreSubject reads one subject. queue_group puts the subscription into the group packers. The server hands each message to one member of a group, so each replica packs a share of the orders. A group name is one group for the server, even across different subjects. A subscription outside the group, or in another group, still gets its own copy.

bill reads the same subject without a group, so it gets every order that pack gets. It bills up to eight orders at once and keeps the order of each customer. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The customer an order belongs to, carried in the partition-key header. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize)] struct CustomerKey { #[serde(rename = "nats-partition-key")] customer: String, } /// The invoice of one order, keyed by the customer like the order it bills. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "invoices.eu", headers = CustomerKey)] struct Invoice { order: u64, amount_cents: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Invoice)] struct Invoices; #[subscriber("orders.eu.created", workers(8, by_key))] async fn bill( order: &Order, Headers(key): Headers<CustomerKey>, Out(invoices): Out<impl Publisher, Invoices>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let invoice = Invoice { order: order.id, amount_cents: order.amount_cents, }; if invoices .message(&invoice) .with_headers(&key) .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } tracing::info!(order.id, customer = %key.customer, "order billed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// The customer an order belongs to, carried in the partition-key header. #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct CustomerKey { #[serde(rename = "nats-partition-key")] customer: String, } /// The invoice of one order, keyed by the customer like the order it bills. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Invoice { order: u64, amount_cents: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Invoice { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "invoices.eu"; } impl MessageHeaders for Invoice { type Contract = WithHeaders<CustomerKey>; } impl MessageInfo for Invoice { const NAME: &'static str = "Invoice"; } struct Invoices; impl OutSlot for Invoices { const NAME: &'static str = "Invoices"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Invoices> for Invoice {} struct Bill; impl<Sent> Handle<Message<CustomerKey, Order>, (), Outs<(Sent,)>> for Bill where Sent: OutEntry<Invoices, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Message<CustomerKey, Order>, outs: &Outs<(Sent,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let key = &order.headers; let invoice = Invoice { order: order.body.id, amount_cents: order.body.amount_cents, }; if outs .get(Invoices) .message(&invoice) .with_headers(key) .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } tracing::info!(order.body.id, customer = %key.customer, "order billed"); Ok(()) } } workers(8, by_key) runs eight lanes. Deliveries with the same key run one after another on one lane. In the manual form the same setting is workers_by_key. NATS has no native key, so the key travels in the nats-partition-key header (PARTITION_KEY_HEADER), and the sender sets it. CustomerKey is a header contract with one field under that name. Headers<CustomerKey> reads the key of the delivery, and with_headers(&key) writes it on the invoice. So the invoices of one customer keep their order for the next reader too. An order without the header fails the contract and is settled by the decode policy, which drops it by default. A NATS header is text: the name is printable ASCII without a colon, and the value is one line. A header that does not fit fails the publish.

audit reads every order event of every region. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(CoreWildcard::new("orders.>"))] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order event audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Audit; impl Handle<Order> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order event audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } CoreWildcard reads every subject a pattern matches. * matches one token: orders.*.created reads the creations of every region. > matches one or more trailing tokens: orders.> reads every subject under orders.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include(pack) .include(bill) .out(Invoices, Publish) // A pattern is no subject to publish a retry copy to, so the mount site names one. .include(audit) .out_retry(Publish) .to("orders.retry") }, ) } src/main.rs fn app() -> impl App<State = ()> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker( NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include( subscriber( CoreSubject::new("orders.eu.created").queue_group("packers"), Pack, ) .build(), ) .include( subscriber("orders.eu.created", Bill) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(8usize)) .build(), ) .out(Invoices, Publish) // A pattern is no subject to publish a retry copy to, so the mount site names one. .include(subscriber(CoreWildcard::new("orders.>"), Audit).build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("orders.retry") }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) } A pattern reads many subjects, so a delayed copy of its delivery has no single subject to go to. The mount site names one with out_retry(Publish).to(..), here orders.retry, which the pattern also reads. Every registration over a pattern names it, even when its handler never retries, and the service refuses to start without it. Retries and dead letters explains the copies.

Core NATS delivers a message to the subscriptions that exist when it arrives. A message published while no subscription matches is gone. A delivery has no acknowledgement either, so a handler that fails does not get the message again from the server. When every message counts, the subject belongs to a stream: Streams and consumers shows how to read one. The tests in the example file run the app in process and check each subscription's copy, the pattern, and the order of the invoices per customer.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp, against an in-process NATS or against a server. The service under test charges card payments. A payment arrives on card.payments, which the stream CARD_PAYMENTS stores, and a durable consumer reads it. The handler replies with a receipt on card.receipts. A payment without a card is dropped. A payment over the bank's instant limit is held: the handler asks for it again in a minute with retry_after. After three deliveries a payment goes to card.review, the dead-letter subject. The app is built by service(broker), so a test chooses the broker's address and main uses the production one. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-nats in [dev-dependencies].

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"))).await?; a_charged_payment_gets_its_receipt(tb).await } async fn a_charged_payment_gets_its_receipt(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .message(&payment(1, 2_500)) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .subscriber("card.payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card.receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_gets_a_receipt() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"))).await?; a_charged_payment_gets_its_receipt(tb).await } async fn a_charged_payment_gets_its_receipt(tb: TestApp<()>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .message(&payment(1, 2_500)) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .subscriber("card.payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card.receipts") .assert_called_once() .with(&Receipt { payment: 1, amount_cents: 2_500, }); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } TestApp::start connects NatsBroker to an in-process NATS. The address is never dialled, and no stream has to be created first. The test addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<NatsBroker>(). message(..).publish() publishes the payment to the subject its type declares, and the stream stores it. publish returns once the handler and its reply have settled. So the next lines assert on finished state: how the subscriber settled and what reached card.receipts. The body takes the started app as an argument, so the live test below runs it too.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_without_a_card_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"))).await?; let no_card = Payment { card: String::new(), ..payment(2, 2_500) }; tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .message(&no_card) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .subscriber("card.payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card.receipts") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_payment_without_a_card_is_dropped() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"))).await?; let no_card = Payment { card: String::new(), ..payment(2, 2_500) }; tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .message(&no_card) .publish() .await?; tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .subscriber("card.payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::drop()); tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .published::<Receipt>("card.receipts") .assert_not_called(); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } settled checks the outcome the handler returned. assert_not_called checks that no receipt was published.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_payment_the_bank_keeps_holding_goes_to_review() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"))).await?; let held = payment(3, 250_000); tb.broker::<NatsBroker>().message(&held).publish().await?; tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .subscriber("card.payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // The consumer holds the payment and delivers it again once `HOLD` has passed. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .subscriber("card.payments") .assert_called(2); // The third delivery is the last one: it goes to the review subject as it arrived. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; assert_eq!( tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .subscriber("card.payments") .outcomes(), [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack], ); tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card.review") .assert_called_once() .with(&held); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)] async fn a_payment_the_bank_keeps_holding_goes_to_review() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let tb = TestApp::start(service(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"))).await?; let held = payment(3, 250_000); tb.broker::<NatsBroker>().message(&held).publish().await?; tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .subscriber("card.payments") .assert_called_once() .settled(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(HOLD)); // The consumer holds the payment and delivers it again once `HOLD` has passed. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .subscriber("card.payments") .assert_called(2); // The third delivery is the last one: it goes to the review subject as it arrived. tb.advance(HOLD).await?; assert_eq!( tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .subscriber("card.payments") .outcomes(), [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Nack], ); tb.broker::<NatsBroker>() .published::<Payment>("card.review") .assert_called_once() .with(&held); tb.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) } The test starts on a paused clock, and advance moves it forward. A minute of HOLD costs nothing. The consumer holds the payment as a server does and delivers it again when the delay ends. The third delivery is the last one the mount site allows, so the payment goes to card.review as it arrived. Each held delivery is recorded as Outcome::Nack.

documents.t: The in-process NATS reads what the client would read: the addresses, and the connection options that change what the server delivers (no_echo, the inbox prefix). It routes and stores as a server does: Subjects match with * and >, and a queue group hands each message to one member. A stream keeps sequences, its duplicate window and the expectations a publish states. A consumer starts where its deliver policy says and carries the metadata of the JetStream context. An acknowledgement, a negative one with or without a delay, and a termination act as on a server; a delivery left unsettled comes back after ack_wait. A request reaches the app's responder, and a request nobody reads gets "no responders" at once. It refuses what the client or the server refuses: a subject with whitespace, a header with no NATS form, a message over 1 MiB, a JetStream publish no stream takes. A stream there stores what the app's consumers read, and a subscription finds every stream it names. A stream's own subject list and limits, max_ack_pending, authentication and TLS need a server.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_payment_gets_a_receipt_on_a_server() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(url) = live::url("NATS_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; // The stream is the server's state: the test creates it, replacing what an interrupted // run left behind, and deletes it afterwards. let admin = NatsBroker::new(url.as_str()).connect().await?; let jetstream = admin.jetstream(); let _ = jetstream.delete_stream("CARD_PAYMENTS").await; jetstream .create_stream(StreamConfig { name: "CARD_PAYMENTS".to_owned(), subjects: vec!["card.payments".to_owned()], ..StreamConfig::default() }) .await?; let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(NatsBroker::new(url.as_str()))).await; let outcome = match tb { Ok(tb) => a_charged_payment_gets_its_receipt(tb).await, Err(err) => Err(err.into()), }; jetstream.delete_stream("CARD_PAYMENTS").await?; admin.shutdown().await?; outcome } src/main.rs #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn a_payment_gets_a_receipt_on_a_server() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let Some(url) = live::url("NATS_TEST_URL") else { return Ok(()); }; // The stream is the server's state: the test creates it, replacing what an interrupted // run left behind, and deletes it afterwards. let admin = NatsBroker::new(url.as_str()).connect().await?; let jetstream = admin.jetstream(); let _ = jetstream.delete_stream("CARD_PAYMENTS").await; jetstream .create_stream(StreamConfig { name: "CARD_PAYMENTS".to_owned(), subjects: vec!["card.payments".to_owned()], ..StreamConfig::default() }) .await?; let tb = TestApp::start_live(service(NatsBroker::new(url.as_str()))).await; let outcome = match tb { Ok(tb) => a_charged_payment_gets_its_receipt(tb).await, Err(err) => Err(err.into()), }; jetstream.delete_stream("CARD_PAYMENTS").await?; admin.shutdown().await?; outcome } TestApp::start_live connects the same app to a running NATS server. The test reads the address from NATS_TEST_URL with live::url, a helper of the example's own, and skips when it is unset. A stream is the server's state, so the test creates CARD_PAYMENTS on a connection of its own first and deletes it afterwards. Deleting the stream also deletes its consumer, so the next run starts clean. The assertions are the in-process ones, unchanged. cargo test NATS_TEST_URL=nats://localhost:4222 cargo test -- --test-threads=1
